chapter: Decca, Cow Cow Blues and royalties
title: Re-recording the same songs, and a pension idea for musicians
summary: Because royalties never arrive he records many versions of the same tunes, and proposes that long-time musicians get an annuity.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: to him that he do to me. I play the same song that I made on another record so he ain't got a damn thing. Just got another version of a song I made. I got five versions of "Honeysuckle Rose," you know that? I got "Willow Weep For Me" three or four times on records. These are things that I've intentionally done. And big companies, they ain't even aware. "I Can't Give You Anything But Love," "Honeysuckle Rose." I made seven records of "Honeysuckle Rose" on different labels. And I do it...well, I like to hear myself play, you know, so I just play the damn thing.Because they ain't going to give you the royalties no way. This is the one thing that I could never understand why artists cannot get their right royalties. You know I think what should happen? That if a man is a musician and he's played, in terms of years, that he should get, like you get Social Security...if he's been a professional musician for ten years or...say if he's been twenty years...then on that twentieth year he should receive, start receiving, some kind of compensation for music that's being played in America. And I think that if they did that that's the fairest way that I can think of. Of course, some guys---a lot of guys got short-changed.--- like Jimmy Blanton and those guys, 'cause they died so early. But I think that every musician that play should in the end get some kind of, you know, some kind
of, you know, some kind of...what do you call it?... honorarium. Annuity, the kind of thing. And they could put it in with his Social Security if he's old enough.
ASCAP has something like that, but it only seems to go to certain people.
